items.stem: Paper 1, Section A. Outline the findings of one study related to the limits of fear-based health campaigns. [4]

Paper 1, Section B (applied short answer). Read the scenario.

A researcher in Accra wants to measure stress in nurses working night shifts and must decide between a questionnaire, saliva cortisol and interviews.

With reference to one relevant study, explain how measurement could be used to understand this situation. [6]
items.answer: each method operationalises stress differently - self-report (subjective, social desirability), cortisol (objective but affected by time of day) and interviews (rich but hard to quantify) - so triangulating methods improves validity

Paper 1, Section B. Scenario: Ji-ho, 17, has a family history of depression. After failing an entrance exam in a highly competitive system, he withdraws and blames himself.

Using psychological research, explain this scenario in terms of the diathesis-stress model. [6]
items.answer: a genetic/cognitive vulnerability (family history, self-blaming style) interacts with a sociocultural stressor (exam pressure and stigma of failure) to trigger depression

items.stem: Paper 1, Section C (extended response). Discuss the view that the brain is shaped more by experience than by genes. Refer to at least two studies. [15]
items.answer: Genes set the basic architecture, but experience continually reshapes networks; both interact.
items.markingKey: Arguments/evidence for: plasticity research (Maguire et al., 2000; Draganski et al., 2004); enriched environments change cortical thickness (Rosenzweig et al., 1972). Arguments/evidence against: basic brain structure is genetically programmed; genes influence plasticity itself; correlational evidence in humans. Possible conclusion: Genes set the basic architecture, but experience continually reshapes networks; both interact. items.stem: Paper 1, Section C (extended response). Evaluate the claim that brain imaging technology has shown that behaviour can be explained by localised brain functions. [15]
items.answer: Imaging supports a degree of localisation, but behaviour is better explained by interacting networks than by single areas.
items.markingKey: Arguments/evidence for: fMRI and lesion studies identify specialised areas (Broca, fusiform face area); split-brain studies show lateralisation (Sperry, 1968). Paper 2, Section B. Read the description of the unseen study "Peer presence and risk-taking".

In a laboratory in Melbourne, 40 university students (aged 18-21) played a computer driving game in which they could stop at amber lights or risk crossing. Each participant played once alone and once with two friends watching; the order was the same for all (alone first). Risky crossings rose from a mean of 4.1 to 7.3 with friends present.

Evaluate this study. In your answer refer to the research design, sampling, measurement, credibility and ethics. [15]
items.answer: repeated measures design controls participant variables; no counterbalancing - practice or boredom effects (order effects) confound peer presence; high control in the lab but low ecological validity: a game is not real driving, no real consequences; sample of university students aged 18-21 - WEIRD, narrow age band; cannot conclude about younger adolescents; friends watching may create demand characteristics; ethics: low risk; informed consent and debriefing required; no deception needed; improvement: counterbalance order, include adolescent and adult age groups (as Gardner and Steinberg, 2005, did)

Paper 3 - Sleep and memory in adolescence. Question 1.

Source A: (Interview extract, hypothetical study of 12 students in Toronto) "When I sleep less than six hours before a test I blank on things I definitely knew... I drink energy drinks so I can stay up revising, but then I remember less." "My phone is the problem. I tell myself one video and then it's 2 a.m."

Identify three factors that the students in Source A believe affect their memory. [3]
items.answer: Short sleep (less than six hours); energy drinks / staying up late revising; phone use delaying sleep.
items.markingKey: Short sleep (less than six hours); energy drinks / staying up late revising; phone use delaying sleep. 1 mark per relevant, accurately identified point from the source (max 3).

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Sleep and memory in adolescence. Question 2.

Source B: (Quantitative data, hypothetical experiment) Mean number of words recalled from a 30-word list after 8 hours' sleep: 18.6 (SD 3.2); after 4 hours' sleep: 13.1 (SD 4.9). n = 24, repeated measures, counterbalanced. Wilcoxon test: p = 0.003.

Interpret the results presented in Source B. [6]
items.answer: Recall was higher after 8 hours (mean 18.6) than after 4 hours (13.1), a difference of 5.5 words; greater SD after 4 hours (4.9 vs 3.2) means less consistent performance; p = 0.003 < 0.05, so the difference is significant and unlikely to be due to chance; the counterbalanced repeated-measures design supports a causal effect of sleep deprivation.
items.markingKey: Recall was higher after 8 hours (mean 18.6) than after 4 hours (13.1), a difference of 5.5 words; greater SD after 4 hours (4.9 vs 3.2) means less consistent performance; p = 0.003 < 0.05, so the difference is significant and unlikely to be due to chance; the counterbalanced repeated-measures design supports a causal effect of sleep deprivation. 5-6: accurate interpretation of the data/text with explicit reference to the source; 3-4: mostly accurate, some reference; 1-2: limited or descriptive.

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Sleep and memory in adolescence. Question 3.

Source C: (Method summary, hypothetical survey) 1,500 adolescents in Lima completed an online survey on bedtime, phone use and self-rated school performance. Later bedtimes correlated with lower self-rated performance (r = -0.29).

Evaluate the research method described in Source C. [6]
items.answer: Strength: large sample, quick, ecologically valid self-reports of real habits. Limitations: correlational - no causation (third variables such as stress or workload); self-rated performance is subjective and prone to social desirability; online sample may exclude students without internet; r = -0.29 is weak; single city limits generalisability.
items.markingKey: Strength: large sample, quick, ecologically valid self-reports of real habits. Limitations: correlational - no causation (third variables such as stress or workload); self-rated performance is subjective and prone to social desirability; online sample may exclude students without internet; r = -0.29 is weak; single city limits generalisability. 5-6: evaluation explicitly applied to the source (method, sample, measurement, credibility, bias); 3-4: relevant but partly generic; 1-2: limited.

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Sleep and memory in adolescence. Question 4.

Source A: (Interview extract, hypothetical study of 12 students in Toronto) "When I sleep less than six hours before a test I blank on things I definitely knew... I drink energy drinks so I can stay up revising, but then I remember less." "My phone is the problem. I tell myself one video and then it's 2 a.m."

Source B: (Quantitative data, hypothetical experiment) Mean number of words recalled from a 30-word list after 8 hours' sleep: 18.6 (SD 3.2); after 4 hours' sleep: 13.1 (SD 4.9). n = 24, repeated measures, counterbalanced. Wilcoxon test: p = 0.003.

Source C: (Method summary, hypothetical survey) 1,500 adolescents in Lima completed an online survey on bedtime, phone use and self-rated school performance. Later bedtimes correlated with lower self-rated performance (r = -0.29).

Using all the sources and your own knowledge, discuss how far the sources support the claim that lack of sleep impairs learning in adolescents. [15]
items.answer: Source B gives the strongest causal evidence (controlled, counterbalanced, significant) but small sample and artificial task; Source C shows the pattern in real life with a large sample but is correlational and self-reported; Source A adds insight into mechanisms (phone use, energy drinks) but is a small qualitative sample. Triangulation across methods strengthens the claim; own knowledge: hippocampus and consolidation, adolescent circadian shift (later melatonin release). Conclusion: well supported for short-term recall, less certain for long-term learning.
items.markingKey: Source B gives the strongest causal evidence (controlled, counterbalanced, significant) but small sample and artificial task; Source C shows the pattern in real life with a large sample but is correlational and self-reported; Source A adds insight into mechanisms (phone use, energy drinks) but is a small qualitative sample. Triangulation across methods strengthens the claim; own knowledge: hippocampus and consolidation, adolescent circadian shift (later melatonin release). Conclusion: well supported for short-term recall, less certain for long-term learning. items.stem: Paper 1, Section A (short answer). Explain how leading questions can distort eyewitness testimony. [4]
items.answer: A leading question introduces post-event information (e.g. "smashed") that either biases the response or alters the stored memory itself, so the witness reconstructs the event in line with the question - as shown by more false reports of broken glass in Loftus and Palmer (1974).
items.markingKey: A leading question introduces post-event information (e.g. "smashed") that either biases the response or alters the stored memory itself, so the witness reconstructs the event in line with the question - as shown by more false reports of broken glass in Loftus and Palmer (1974). 4 marks: clear, accurate explanation with a relevant example or study; 2-3 marks: partial explanation; 1 mark: relevant point stated.

Paper 2, Section B. Read the description of the unseen study "Screen time and toddlers".

Researchers in Seoul asked 120 parents of two-year-olds (recruited at three private clinics) to complete an online questionnaire estimating their child's daily screen time and to rate their child's vocabulary using a checklist. Paper 3 - Social media and well-being. Question 1.

Source A: (Focus group extract, hypothetical study, Oslo) "I compare myself with influencers and feel ugly." "Group chats are how I keep my friends - without them I'd be lonely." "Likes make me check my phone all the time."

Identify three effects of social media described by the participants in Source A. [3]
items.answer: Upward social comparison leading to negative body image ("feel ugly"); maintaining friendships / reducing loneliness through group chats; compulsive checking driven by likes (reward).
items.markingKey: Upward social comparison leading to negative body image ("feel ugly"); maintaining friendships / reducing loneliness through group chats; compulsive checking driven by likes (reward). 1 mark per relevant, accurately identified point from the source (max 3).

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Social media and well-being. Question 2.

Source B: (Quantitative data, hypothetical experiment) Students randomly allocated to limit social media to 30 minutes a day for 3 weeks (n = 70) reported a fall in loneliness scores from 42.1 to 36.4; the control group (n = 73) changed from 41.8 to 41.2. Mann-Whitney U test: p = 0.02.

Interpret the findings presented in Source B. [6]
items.answer: The limited group's loneliness fell by 5.7 points vs 0.6 in controls; p = 0.02 < 0.05 so the difference between groups is significant; random allocation supports a causal conclusion that reducing use lowers loneliness, at least over 3 weeks.
items.markingKey: The limited group's loneliness fell by 5.7 points vs 0.6 in controls; p = 0.02 < 0.05 so the difference between groups is significant; random allocation supports a causal conclusion that reducing use lowers loneliness, at least over 3 weeks. 5-6: accurate interpretation of the data/text with explicit reference to the source; 3-4: mostly accurate, some reference; 1-2: limited or descriptive.

Paper 3 - Social media and well-being. Question 3.

Source C: (Method summary, hypothetical longitudinal study) 3,000 Canadian adolescents completed yearly questionnaires for four years. Increases in a teenager's social media use were followed by small increases in depressive symptoms the following year (β = 0.07).

Evaluate the research method used in Source C. [6]
items.answer: Strengths: large sample, longitudinal - shows temporal order (use precedes symptoms), within-person change. Limitations: still correlational - third variables (e.g. stress, family conflict); self-report; very small effect size (β = 0.07); attrition over four years; one culture.

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Social media and well-being. Question 4.

Source A: (Focus group extract, hypothetical study, Oslo) "I compare myself with influencers and feel ugly." "Group chats are how I keep my friends - without them I'd be lonely." "Likes make me check my phone all the time."

Source B: (Quantitative data, hypothetical experiment) Students randomly allocated to limit social media to 30 minutes a day for 3 weeks (n = 70) reported a fall in loneliness scores from 42.1 to 36.4; the control group (n = 73) changed from 41.8 to 41.2. Mann-Whitney U test: p = 0.02.

Source C: (Method summary, hypothetical longitudinal study) 3,000 Canadian adolescents completed yearly questionnaires for four years. Increases in a teenager's social media use were followed by small increases in depressive symptoms the following year (β = 0.07).

Using all the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that social media use harms adolescents' well-being. [15]
items.answer: A shows both harmful (comparison) and beneficial (connection) effects; B provides experimental support for a causal effect but short duration and student sample; C suggests a small longitudinal effect. Own knowledge: social comparison theory, dopamine and variable reinforcement, displacement of sleep. Conclusion: effects are real but small and depend on how social media is used; "harms" is too general.

items.stem: Paper 1, Section A. Describe one study investigating the social origins of depression. [4]
items.answer: For example Brown and Harris (1978): aim to investigate social factors associated with depression in women; method: Interviews with 458 women in Camberwell, London, about life events, difficulties and depression over the previous year. Findings: severe life events and difficulties triggered depression, especially in women with vulnerability factors such as lack of an intimate relationship or three or more children under 14 at home

items.stem: Paper 1, Section A (short answer). Explain why adoption studies help separate genetic and environmental influences. [4]
items.answer: Adopted children share genes with biological parents but environment with adoptive parents, so similarity to biological parents suggests genetic influence and similarity to adoptive parents suggests environmental influence.

items.stem:
Paper 1, Section B. Scenario: After a stroke, Elena's left arm is weak; her therapist restrains her right arm for several hours a day so she must use the weak arm repeatedly.

Using psychological research, explain this scenario in terms of neuroplasticity. [6]
items.answer: forced, repeated use of the weak limb promotes cortical reorganisation so undamaged areas take over motor control

items.stem:
Paper 1, Section B (applied short answer). Read the scenario.

Omar, 19, in Dubai, finds he craves a cigarette whenever he is stressed; nicotine stimulates acetylcholine receptors and increases dopamine release in the reward pathway.

With reference to one relevant study, explain how neurotransmitters and behaviour could be used to understand this situation. [6]
items.answer: nicotine acts as an agonist that increases dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, reinforcing smoking and producing craving

items.stem: Paper 1, Section C (extended response). "Human decision-making is fundamentally irrational." To what extent do you agree? Refer to research in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Decision-making is boundedly rational: biases are real, but heuristics are often effective in real environments.
items.markingKey: Arguments/evidence for: anchoring, framing, availability biases are robust; predictable deviations from rational choice. Arguments/evidence against: heuristics are adaptive ("ecological rationality", Gigerenzer); lab problems are artificial; experts often decide well in familiar domains. Possible conclusion: Decision-making is boundedly rational: biases are real, but heuristics are often effective in real environments. items.stem: Paper 1, Section C (extended response). Discuss the view that evolutionary explanations of behaviour are not scientific. Refer to at least two studies. [15]
items.answer: Evolutionary explanations can be scientific when they make specific, testable predictions, but many are speculative and need cultural evidence.

Paper 2, practical-based question (data). Directional hypothesis: reaction times in milliseconds on a Stroop colour-naming trial will be higher for incongruent colour words than for congruent colour words.

Condition A (for incongruent colour words): 913, 589, 937, 809, 744, 584
Condition B (for congruent colour words): 980, 609, 980, 850, 829, 601

Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation for each condition (to 2 decimal places). State whether the descriptive statistics are in the direction predicted by the hypothesis and compare the spread of the two conditions.
items.answer: Mean A = 762.67, SD A = 153.34; mean B = 808.17, SD B = 169.60. The means are not in the predicted direction. Condition B has the larger SD, so its scores are more spread out (less consistent). Descriptive statistics alone cannot show that the difference is significant; an inferential test is needed.
items.markingKey: A1 means: A = 4576/6 = 762.67, B = 4849/6 = 808.17. A1 SD A = 153.34. A1 SD B = 169.60. R1 direction: does not support the hypothesis. R1 spread: condition B is more variable.

items.stem: Paper 2, practical-based question. Explain why you chose to use a covert or an overt observation in your class practical. [5]
items.answer: Justifies the choice: covert reduces participant reactivity (Hawthorne effect) but raises consent issues and is only acceptable in public settings; overt is more ethical but behaviour may change; links to the specific setting observed.

items.stem:
Paper 2, Section B. Read the description of the unseen study "Mindfulness app and stress".

A technology company in Singapore tested its own mindfulness app. Employees who signed up for the app (n = 85) completed the Perceived Stress Scale before and after 6 weeks of use. Mean scores fell from 22.0 to 17.5. No control group was used. The company advertised that the app "reduces stress by 20%".

Evaluate this study. In your answer refer to the research design, sampling, measurement, credibility and ethics. [15]
items.answer: repeated measures but no control group - changes could be due to time, regression to the mean or placebo/expectancy effects; self-selected sample: motivated employees; drop-outs not reported (attrition bias); funding bias / conflict of interest - the company tested its own product; researcher not independent; PSS is a standardised, reliable measure - a strength; the 20% claim uses the drop in mean (4.5/22 = about 20%) but not significance or clinical meaning; ethics: workplace pressure to participate; confidentiality of health data; improvement: randomised controlled trial with waiting-list control, independent researchers, follow-up
items.markingKey: Indicative content: repeated measures but no control group - changes could be due to time, regression to the mean or placebo/expectancy effects; self-selected sample: motivated employees; drop-outs not reported (attrition bias); funding bias / conflict of interest - the company tested its own product; researcher not independent; PSS is a standardised, reliable measure - a strength; the 20% claim uses the drop in mean (4.5/22 = about 20%) but not significance or clinical meaning; ethics: workplace pressure to participate; confidentiality of health data; improvement: randomised controlled trial with waiting-list control, independent researchers, follow-up. Markbands (15): 13-15 - evaluation is focused on THIS study: design, sampling, measurement, control of variables, credibility/bias, generalisability and ethics are each explained with explicit reference to details in the stimulus; strengths and limitations are weighed and realistic improvements are justified. 10-12 - several relevant, mostly well-explained points linked to the stimulus. 7-9 - relevant points, some generic or not linked to the stimulus. 4-6 - mainly generic evaluation with limited reference to the study. 1-3 - very limited, largely descriptive. Generic points not applied to the study (e.g. "small sample") cannot reach the top bands.

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Acculturation and stress in international students. Question 1.

Source A: (Interview extract, hypothetical study of 10 students from Ghana studying in Vienna) "At home elders decide with you; here everyone wants you to decide alone." "Speaking German in class makes me anxious." "The African student association feels like family."

Identify three sources of acculturative stress or support mentioned in Source A. [3]
items.answer: Differences in cultural norms (collectivist vs individualist decision making); language anxiety; social support from a co-national student association.
items.markingKey: Differences in cultural norms (collectivist vs individualist decision making); language anxiety; social support from a co-national student association. 1 mark per relevant, accurately identified point from the source (max 3).

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Acculturation and stress in international students. Question 2.

Source B: (Quantitative data, hypothetical survey, n = 240 international students) Acculturation strategy and mean acculturative stress (1-5): integration 2.1; assimilation 2.8; separation 3.0; marginalisation 3.9.

Interpret the data in Source B with reference to Berry's acculturation model. [6]
items.answer: Stress is lowest for integration (2.1) and highest for marginalisation (3.9), with assimilation and separation in between - consistent with Berry (1997) that maintaining heritage culture while engaging with the host culture is the most adaptive strategy; but the data are correlational and stress may also influence strategy.
items.markingKey: Stress is lowest for integration (2.1) and highest for marginalisation (3.9), with assimilation and separation in between - consistent with Berry (1997) that maintaining heritage culture while engaging with the host culture is the most adaptive strategy; but the data are correlational and stress may also influence strategy. 5-6: accurate interpretation of the data/text with explicit reference to the source; 3-4: mostly accurate, some reference; 1-2: limited or descriptive.

items.stem:
Paper 3 - Acculturation and stress in international students. Question 3.

Source C: (Method summary) Researchers translated an English acculturation questionnaire into Korean, Arabic and Spanish without back-translation and gave it to students during orientation week.

Evaluate the method described in Source C. [6]
items.answer: No back-translation risks non-equivalence of meaning (imposed etic, measurement bias); orientation week is atypical (early in the process, high excitement or stress); questionnaire allows a large sample and comparison; suggest back-translation, pilot testing, and measuring at several time points.

Paper 3 - Acculturation and stress in international students. Question 4.

Source A: (Interview extract, hypothetical study of 10 students from Ghana studying in Vienna) "At home elders decide with you; here everyone wants you to decide alone." "Speaking German in class makes me anxious." "The African student association feels like family."

Source C: (Method summary) Researchers translated an English acculturation questionnaire into Korean, Arabic and Spanish without back-translation and gave it to students during orientation week.

Using all the sources and your own knowledge, discuss what the sources suggest about the relationship between acculturation and mental health. [15]
items.answer: Synthesises A (qualitative mechanisms: norms, language, support), B (pattern consistent with Berry), C (measurement concerns that weaken B-type evidence). Own knowledge: Lueck and Wilson (2010) - language discrimination and family conflict increase stress, bilingualism protects. Conclusion: integration is associated with better outcomes, but causality and measurement equivalence are uncertain.
